ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly short-to-medium conversational turns before and after the formal presentations, with long, structured monologues during talks and comparatively extended, exploratory answers in Q&A. Openings are casual and socially warm, featuring repeated greetings, side chatter, and technical check-ins; overlap and quick backchanneling (“yeah,” “okay,” “right,” laughter-like reactions) are frequent, especially in transitions. Participants speak informally but professionally, using many hesitations, restarts, repetitions, and self-corrections (“um,” “I mean,” “you know,” “sort of,” “I think”), with uncertainty framed gently through phrases like “maybe,” “it could be,” “we’re interested in,” and “I don’t know.” Questions are usually prefaced with praise or disclaimers such as “great talk,” “quick question,” or “naive question,” then unfold as multi-part, conversational prompts rather than tightly scripted interrogations. Challenges are indirect and collaborative: speakers raise alternative interpretations, limitations, or follow-ups without adversarial phrasing, and presenters tend to validate the question before answering at length. The overall rhythm alternates between relaxed collegial banter, formal seminar-style exposition, and friendly, technically engaged discussion.

Meeting style for this meeting (quick_checkin): A rushed weekly check-in. People give short status updates and ask each other quick questions. Most turns are one or two sentences. Nobody summarizes. Someone has another meeting soon and the conversation stops where it stops.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Okay, so, quick one from me- the export finished last night, mostly.
  - Mostly?
  - Two of the sites didn't come through. I haven't looked yet.
Opening: Start with one person already reading from, or referring to, a document the others have open.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Introducing a risk-scoring model to help community clinics decide which patients to call first.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Fourth-year PhD candidate in clinical machine learning, with three years embedded in a health-system data science group. She helped validate the outreach-risk model using retrospective electronic health record data, focusing on calibration curves, sensitivity at operational thresholds, and reproducible scoring pipelines. She has experience translating model outputs into simple clinic-facing tools but has not led frontline clinic operations.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Treats the score as a probabilistic prioritization instrument whose practical value depends on whether its ranking remains adequately calibrated and sensitive in use. She favors deploying the existing validated model for a bounded pilot rather than extending development, while using the three-month review to inspect performance in the pilot setting.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language

speakers.name: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
speakers.background: Associate professor of epidemiology with 14 years of experience evaluating care-management and emergency-department prevention programs in safety-net settings. His work uses quasi-experimental designs, historical comparison cohorts, outcome ascertainment from linked hospital feeds, and pragmatic implementation measures. He has partnered with rural clinics on protocol development and understands the constraints of sparse staffing and routine data collection.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames the pilot as a pragmatic evaluation: define an outcome that can be consistently observed, specify a comparable historical reference group from the same clinics, and document enough process information to interpret results. He emphasizes that an emergency department visit within 30 days is observable through the available feed, while outreach and subsequent clinic-record appearances provide useful implementation indicators.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Lena Brooks
speakers.background: Professor of medical sociology and principal investigator for the pilot, with 18 years studying how frontline workers adopt decision-support tools in community health organizations. She uses qualitative interviews, observation, workflow mapping, and organizational ethnography to examine discretion, trust, language access, and the social consequences of categorization. Her prior projects include outreach programs serving immigrant and rural populations.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Examines the ranked list as an organizational artifact rather than a neutral output: staff may experience it as an instruction, and patients' reachability is shaped by phone instability, language needs, prior institutional experiences, and trust. She seeks safeguards that preserve staff discretion and make non-call decisions visible through lightweight documentation, while deferring to technical and epidemiologic colleagues on model metrics and outcome measurement.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

seed_spec.explicit_instruction:
Hold a planning meeting with Dr. Maya Chen (computer science), Dr. Rafael Ortiz (epidemiology), and Dr. Lena Brooks (sociology), plus clinic operations lead Jordan Patel. The group must make these final decisions: use the existing model without retraining for the six-month pilot; send the top 25 patients per clinic each weekday to outreach staff; define the primary outcome as any emergency department visit within 30 days of list generation; assess performance after three months using available clinic and hospital-feed records; and give staff a brief orientation stating that the score is a prioritization aid rather than a directive.

Dr. Chen should state that the model was calibrated in the development system, that a three-month review will examine overall calibration and sensitivity, and that using the existing model avoids delaying the pilot. Dr. Ortiz should state that the outcome is measurable from the available hospital feed, that pilot patients should be compared with historical patients from the same clinics, and that the team will record whether a patient appears in clinic records after receiving a list. Dr. Brooks should raise that staff may interpret a ranked list as an instruction and that some patients may be hard to reach because of phone instability, language needs, or distrust; after discussion, she accepts the orientation and proposes asking staff to log a short reason when they do not call someone. Jordan should state that 25 calls is the operational limit and that staff may reorder or skip names based on local knowledge.

Ensure the final decisions are clear. Include evidence supporting both stated assumptions and reasonable unstated assumptions embedded in the decisions. Do not have participants label assumptions, enumerate them, or perform an assumptions analysis. Do not introduce a hidden flaw, conflict, or missing-data issue beyond the stated limits; any unresolved limitations should be ordinary and visible in the discussion.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: I’m looking at the protocol draft—sorry, page three is still showing the old clinic names for me, but that’s minor. For today, I’d really like us to get the daily list-and-call workflow nailed down, and enough of the evaluation plan so leadership can see what we’ll actually be able to learn in six months.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: On the workflow, I think we should use the existing model for the six-month pilot. I was going to say without retraining because it was calibrated in the development system, but really, reopening development would delay us. The daily output is a ranked probability list, not a prediction that any one person will go to the ED, so a top-25 starting list seems operationally clean. Jordan, when staff reorder it, what local information are they usually using?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: I’d want the orientation to say explicitly that the score is a prioritization aid, not a directive. Staff may still experience a ranked list as an instruction, though. Jordan, what are the ordinary legitimate reasons they already use to reorder or skip names, and could they log a very short reason when they don’t call someone?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: The top 25 works as a default, as long as the reorderings and skips leave a small routine trace, and if they don't then...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That trace is important, especially around the cutoff, where nearby scores can be very close.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: Right—otherwise the rank starts functioning like a mandate, especially at that cutoff.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: Mm, especially near the cutoff.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Yeah—I'd want staff to see those near-cutoff cases as interchangeable enough to use judgment.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: The orientation should make that interchangeability explicit, not just tell people to use judgment in the abstract. I’m also wondering whether each clinic actually has routine interpreter or language-concordant calling available for the languages they see, because language need, phone instability, or distrust can otherwise quietly become reasons a name falls down the list.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Hm, that’s important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: For the evaluation, I'd keep the primary outcome really plain. Any emergency department visit within 30 days of list generation. That's the one outcome the available hospital feed should let us observe consistently, though I still need to confirm the refresh timing and completeness with the feed team.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That works if the feed is linkable back to the daily scoring files on a stable patient identifier—otherwise we can’t tell which generated lists led to which 30-day outcomes. Rafael, when you check completeness, could you also check that linkage? At three months I’ll examine overall calibration and sensitivity, but I’d want to describe it cautiously until we know the outcome count.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: I'll check both the identifier linkage and what the feed actually captures over those 30 days. Maya, when you say calibration for leadership, what summary feels, feels legible but still honest about whether predicted risks line up with what we observe here?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I’d keep it pretty simple. A calibration plot that compares predicted risk with observed 30-day ED use, probably in a few broad risk groups rather than pretending we have precision at every score. Then sensitivity at the operational top-25 threshold, or I should say, what share of observed events were on a list. Though at three months, that’s an interim signal, not a verdict.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: That feels right. I'd put the broad-group plot in the three-month review alongside the actual number of 30-day events, so nobody reads a wobbly calibration curve as more certain than it is. And we can assess it from the clinic and hospital-feed records. For the outcome comparison, I still want historical patients from these same clinics as the practical— I mean, as the reference point we can actually use.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: I’d be a little cautious about treating the historical comparison as a clean reference, because the list changes the work process as well as who gets called. Could we at least retain the short skip or, uh, reorder codes and a clinic-record appearance indicator, Rafael, so we can distinguish someone who was never reached by phone from someone who later engaged in another way? Otherwise, “not engaged” can become a pretty misleading category.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: Exactly. I’d record whether a patient shows up in the clinic record after they get a list, but I wouldn’t call that successful outreach unless the call documentation backs it up. Lena, what would a short non-call reason capture well enough here, and what would it miss about the encounter or other kinds of contact?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: The code can capture the immediate operational reason, like already contacted, known language-access need, no working phone, patient preference or safety concern, competing clinical urgency, or staff judgment that someone else should go first. It will miss the texture of why, especially distrust or a family-mediated or in-person contact pathway. So I’d avoid collapsing those into “not engaged,” and the clinic-record indicator gives us a useful second trace.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: That’s useful. The codes tell us why the planned call didn’t happen, and then the later clinic-record appearance tells us not to mistake that for no contact at all. I’d keep the codes very short, and optional only when the reason genuinely isn’t, um, knowable. Otherwise we’ll lose the interpretability we need for the historical same-clinic comparison.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: And from the scoring side, those codes matter too because they tell us whether the top-25 workflow was actually applied, rather than making a skipped patient look like a model failure. I’d avoid making “staff judgment” too broad if we can. Maybe it’s a usable code, but we should be able to see how often it’s, um, doing the work.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: I’d keep “staff judgment,” but where it’s feasible, pair it with a one-click subtype, like clinical context, prior relationship, or anticipated reachability, instead of asking for a narrative. The important thing is that discretion doesn’t disappear analytically. It’s doing real work in this setting, and we should be able to see when it’s concentrated around language access or unstable contact information.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Yeah, that granularity helps.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: I like that. If we can see those subtypes by clinic and by whether the person later appears in the clinic record, we get some purchase on whether the workflow is systematically leaving certain patients out, without pretending a one-click code explains the whole encounter and...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: And I’d want us to look at those patterns without treating anticipated reachability as a patient trait. It may be a record of the clinic’s contact infrastructure, like phone turnover, interpreter availability, prior experience with us, so could the orientation tell staff that explicitly, even briefly, or...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: I'd put that directly in the orientation. Anticipated reachability is information about the contact system, not a fixed attribute of the patient. Then in the three-month review, we can look at those codes by language need and clinic, alongside later clinic-record appearances, as a workflow signal rather than attributing it to patients.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: And analytically, we should keep that separate from the score itself. If anticipated reachability is driving, driving reorderings, I'd want the three-month review to show that alongside the score distribution, so we don't mistake a contact-system constraint for a calibration problem.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: When we do the three-month review, I'd want that shown next to the basic outcome count and the historical same-clinic reference, not folded into it. If reorderings are mostly about reachability, that changes how we interpret both the observed ED rate and any, any apparent calibration drift.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: Right, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Yeah, exactly—that separation will make the interim performance read much more interpretable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: Okay, I think we're at time. I'll check the feed details, and we can pick this back up once those are clear—thanks, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: Great, bye all—talk soon.
